column9: Zohar, Tetzaveh 10:83-11:92: ‘In the Zohar (Tetzaveh II 184a), Rabbi Shimon expounds: “Why did the Holy One, blessed be He, send Israel down into the darkness of exile? Because there is no true light except that which emerges from within darkness (de-leit nehora ela hahu de-nafik mi-go chashokha), and there is no true good except that which is recognized from within evil (ve-leit tava ela hahu de-nafik mi-go bisha).”’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: This foundational Zoharic principle explains why Hashem derives satisfaction even from what appears opposite to the good: from the very first utterance of Creation, the Supernal Thought ordained that darkness precede light so that when man overcomes darkness through repentance out of love, a far higher light shines forth.

column9: Bereshit Rabbah 11: ‘“Which God created to make (la’asot)” (Genesis 2:3): Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov said: Everything that was created during the six days of Creation requires further human preparation and action—for example, mustard needs to be sweetened, lupines need to be sweetened, wheat needs to be ground and baked, and even man himself requires rectification (tikkun) through circumcision and the commandments.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok reads the infinitive la’asot (‘to make’) at the close of Vayechulu through Bereshit Rabbah 11:6: God deliberately left creation unfinished so that human beings would become active partners in rectifying and sweetening both the physical world and their own souls.
column11: Just as a slave's ear is pierced as a sign of permanent servitude, so circumcision is a sign that the entire body is bound in service to the Blessed One even apart from one's conscious will. That is: even when his actions and expressed will appear otherwise, the truth of his innermost will remains so. Therefore on Purim one is obligated to become intoxicated until he does not know, for then a person is revealed through his cup: he acts only according to the power implanted within him, with no restraint upon his spirit.

column9: Midrash Tanchuma, Tazria 5: ‘Turnus Rufus the wicked asked Rabbi Akiva: “Whose works are more beautiful, those of the Holy One, blessed be He, or those of flesh and blood?” Rabbi Akiva replied: “Those of flesh and blood are more beautiful!” When Turnus Rufus challenged him over circumcision, Rabbi Akiva brought him stalks of wheat and fine baked cakes of bread, saying: “These stalks are the work of the Holy One, blessed be He, and these cakes are the work of flesh and blood—are not the cakes finer?” Turnus Rufus said: “If God desires circumcision, why does the infant not emerge circumcised from his mother’s womb?” Rabbi Akiva answered: “Because the Holy One, blessed be He, gave the commandments to Israel solely in order to refine and purify them through their own action!”’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok cites Rabbi Akiva’s famous disputation with Turnus Rufus in Tanchuma Tazria 5 to prove that human effort in rectifying oneself—symbolized by circumcision and repentance out of love—is precisely what makes creation most beautiful before Hashem.

How many bitter and harsh herbs exist in the world—such as mustard, capers, and lupines—that are far more bitter than the Evil Inclination, yet you know how to boil and sweeten them for your benefit! For prayer is the immediate perception of the divine Presence, standing as one before the King, as written in Eruvin 64a, meaning the steadfast focus of heart and mind; for the Blessed Name looks into the heart, and if, Heaven forbid, an alien thought or external musing befalls him, he is not standing at that instant before Him.
